stories.headline: Trump rejects Iranian seven day plan to reopen Hormuz
stories.dek: Iran tied reopening the strait to a wider ceasefire, while the US kept up sanctions and allies tightened transport and banking links.
paragraphs: President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. Iran had linked the step to a broader halt in fighting across the Middle East and other conditions from earlier failed ceasefire talks. The refusal matters now because shipping through the strait remains under pressure.

The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that carries a large share of the world's oil and gas shipments. Iran says it is still waiting for mediators to pass on a final US position. At the same time, Washington is pushing other countries to cut Iranian banking and airline links.

It is still unclear whether Oman or other mediators can revive talks, or whether Iran will ease restrictions without a wider deal. Gulf states want normal shipping restored with no new fees or controls. For now, the route remains a point of leverage in a wider regional war.
stories.changes: It raises the chance of longer delays, higher freight costs, and more tension around energy shipments through the Gulf.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the strait is fully closed or that a wider regional settlement is off the table.

cover.title: Trump rejects Iran plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
cover.standfirst: President Donald Trump turned down an Iranian offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. Iran had tied the move to a wider Middle East ceasefire and other conditions, while the US pressed allies to cut Iranian flights, banks and trade links as mediation efforts continue.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Show the Strait of Hormuz from above as a narrow white channel between two flat landmasses, with the lower third left as quiet blue water for type. A single tanker is entering the choke point, but its hull is unmistakably the White House stretched into ship form; at the exact mouth of the strait its bow is already swinging away, carving a clean turning wake, while two or three tiny ordinary escort boats continue straight toward the gap beneath and past it. Keep the forms blunt and graphic in federal blue, white and fluorescent pink so the refusal reads instantly and the second read is that Washington itself has become the vessel refusing passage.
art.note: Tense and spare, with dusty sand, deep blue, and one hard red accent.
art.second_beat: First you see a ship turning back at Hormuz; then you realize the ship is the White House, so the blocked reopening is specifically Washington’s refusal, not generic disruption.

stories.headline: Palestinian death toll in Gaza war passes 74000
stories.dek: Gaza's Health Ministry said 74,016 Palestinians have been killed since the war began in October 2023.
paragraphs: Gaza's Health Ministry said Saturday that 74,016 Palestinians have been killed in the war, with 175,068 wounded. The new total matters because it marks another major threshold in a conflict that has continued despite an October 10 ceasefire that stopped the heaviest fighting but not all Israeli strikes.

The war began on October 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked Israel, killing about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and taking 251 hostages. Gaza's Health Ministry is part of the Hamas-run government, but its casualty records are generally treated as reliable by UN agencies and other international organisations.

Much of the ceasefire remains stuck. The ministry says 1,145 Palestinians have been killed since it took effect, while Israel says seven soldiers have died in the same period. Israeli forces still control more than half of Gaza, Hamas has not disarmed, no new Palestinian government has taken over, and reconstruction has not started.
stories.changes: For readers, the update shows that people are still being killed in Gaza even after a ceasefire reduced the main battles.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the war has fully resumed at its earlier intensity or that a political settlement is any closer.

cover.title: Gaza war death toll passes 74000 despite ceasefire
cover.standfirst: Gaza's Health Ministry said 74,016 Palestinians have been killed and 175,068 wounded since the war began in October 2023. A ceasefire that started on October 10 stopped the biggest battles, but Israeli strikes have continued and key terms of the truce remain unresolved.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: A near-black engraved field is filled edge to edge with dense vertical tally cuts incised into a rough wall, the marks packed so tightly they also read as a burial ground of upright grave markers or tightly lined shrouds. In the upper half, a burin is caught mid-incision making one fresh bright stroke, the new cut gleaming white and slightly raw against the older marks; keep the lower third quieter, with fewer cuts and more open black, so type can sit across it. No extra symbols, no figures, no text—just the wall, the tool, and the newest wound-like mark being added.
art.note: Silent, heavy, ash-grey and sand tones.
art.second_beat: First it is a count being updated; a beat later the tally wall becomes a field of graves, and the act of recording is revealed as another wound.

stories.headline: Police evacuate homes near RAF Fairford and detain several men
stories.dek: Bomb disposal experts examined vehicles after arrests under the Explosives Act near the U.S.-used air base in Gloucestershire.
paragraphs: British police evacuated homes near RAF Fairford on Sunday after arresting several men on suspicion of explosives offences. Army bomb disposal experts were sent to examine several vehicles. The operation was treated as a major incident because the base is used by U.S. forces and access points were sealed off.

RAF Fairford in southwest England has been authorised by Britain for U.S. strikes on Iranian missile sites linked to attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned in July that any base used for such strikes could be treated as a legitimate target.

Police have not said how many men were detained, what was found in the vehicles, or whether the case is linked to any foreign threat. The U.S. Air Force said only that it was taking appropriate security measures. Residents do not yet know when they can return home.

cover.title: Police evacuate homes near RAF Fairford and detain several men
cover.standfirst: Bomb disposal experts examined vehicles after arrests under the Explosives Act near the U.S.-used air base in Gloucestershire.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat signal-red ground, a bomb-disposal technician in a bulky EOD suit strides hard left-to-right, cropped slightly by the right edge so the figure feels mid-operation rather than posed. Render the suit as a brutal black cutout with the robot-controller box and cable clear in hand; inside the black torso and visor, carve a stark white negative-space silhouette of a semi-detached suburban house with pitched roof and chimney, clean and unmistakable. Keep the lower third largely empty red for type, with the figure crossing above it.
art.second_beat: First you see the explosives officer in motion; a beat later the white void inside the suit resolves into an evacuated home, showing the bomb search entering ordinary domestic life.

stories.headline: Bangkok flooding pushes thousands into shelters after disaster declaration
stories.dek: Nearly 4,900 people were evacuated and about 52,000 households were affected as flooding spread across parts of the Thai capital.
paragraphs: Flooding in Bangkok has forced nearly 4,900 people into shelters and affected about 52,000 households. Authorities declared a disaster as water spread through parts of the city. The declaration signals that the flooding is serious enough to require emergency help and coordinated response now.

Bangkok is a low-lying city that is vulnerable to flooding during periods of heavy rain. Large numbers of homes can be disrupted even when water does not cover the whole city. Evacuations and shelters are used when people cannot safely remain in their homes.

It is not yet clear how quickly floodwaters will recede or whether more evacuations will follow. The summary does not say which districts were hit hardest, how long shelters will stay open, or how much damage homes, roads, and local services have suffered.
stories.changes: For residents in affected areas, daily travel, work, and access to home may be disrupted while emergency shelters and flood response continue.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all of Bangkok is underwater or that the entire city has stopped functioning.

cover.title: Bangkok floods force thousands into shelters across the city
cover.standfirst: Flooding in Bangkok has pushed nearly 4,900 people into shelters and affected about 52,000 households. Authorities declared a disaster as water spread through parts of the Thai capital. It is still unclear how long the flooding will last or whether more evacuations will be needed.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint one unmistakably Bangkok shophouse street in a single wide gouache view, with the floodwater itself making the split: above the brown waterline, the remembered dry city—parked motorbikes, a food cart tucked under an awning, dense black utility wires, open shopfronts; below it, the exact same facades continue into their flooded present as reflections and submersion, with the cart gone, shutters half-drowned, and one small rescue boat guiding evacuees through the same corridor of buildings. Keep the lower third mostly broad floodwater and soft reflections so type can sit there; use just one boat, a few figures, and the repeated shopfronts to make the transformation legible at a glance.
art.note: Muted grey-blue and muddy brown palette, calm but urgent mood.
art.second_beat: First you see a flooded Bangkok street; then you realize the image is holding the same block in two states at once, so the flood reads as an edit imposed on ordinary city life.

stories.headline: Rare early-season storm hits northeastern United States hard
stories.dek: The storm has battered the East Coast since Saturday, cutting power to thousands of homes and leaving one person dead.
paragraphs: A powerful storm has hit the northeastern United States since Saturday, bringing dangerous weather to the East Coast. The system is unusual for this time of year. It has knocked out electricity to thousands of homes and businesses. Authorities have also reported one death linked to the storm.

The US Northeast often faces major storms in winter and during hurricane season, but a strong system outside those periods is less common. The region includes dense cities, older power lines and coastal areas that flood easily. That makes even a short storm disruptive for transport, power and daily life.

It is not yet clear how long outages will last or whether the death toll will rise. Officials still need to assess damage across several states. Weather conditions may also continue to affect travel and repairs. Residents are waiting for fuller forecasts and local emergency updates.
stories.changes: For many readers in the region, this means possible power cuts, travel delays and a need to follow local weather and emergency advice.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean every part of the US East Coast is in crisis, or that unusual weather has shut down the whole region.

cover.title: Rare storm cuts power across the northeastern United States
cover.standfirst: A powerful storm has hit the US East Coast since Saturday in an unusual burst of severe weather for the season. Thousands of homes and businesses have lost electricity and one person has died. Officials are still measuring damage and working to restore power as the system moves through the region.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint a simplified map of the northeastern U.S. coast from Pennsylvania through New England, with Long Island and Cape Cod unmistakable, in flat calm coastal color blocks. Across it, a single National Weather Service-style spiral rain band sweeps diagonally northeastward — but on second look the entire band is made of whipping black power lines and extension cords, with a few plugs and snapped ends just enough to identify them; keep the lower third mostly quiet as open sea for type. The cords should have real storm motion, arcing and tangling as if the blackout itself is the weather system.
art.note: Cold, wind-beaten mood; slate gray, deep blue and muted green palette.
art.second_beat: First you read a storm radar image; a beat later you realize the storm band is made of downed electrical lines, fusing the unusual early storm with the outages it caused.

stories.headline: Avalanche on Nepal mountain leaves at least 10 people missing
stories.dek: Rescuers are searching Himlung Himal after an avalanche hit during persistent rain and snowfall across Nepal.
paragraphs: At least 10 people are missing after an avalanche on Himlung Himal in Nepal, according to local reports carried by international broadcasters. The accident came as persistent rain and snowfall hit parts of the country, worsening conditions in the mountains and adding pressure to rescue efforts.

Himlung Himal is a high Himalayan peak in northern Nepal, where climbing and trekking routes can be exposed to sudden weather changes. The same spell of bad weather has also triggered landslides and flooding elsewhere in Nepal. At least one person has been reported killed outside the avalanche zone.

It is not yet clear who the missing people are, whether they were climbers or support staff, or how quickly rescuers can reach them. Officials still need to confirm the full toll from the avalanche and from the wider flooding and landslides as rain and snow continue.
stories.changes: For travelers and families in Nepal, mountain routes and some roads may become more dangerous and more likely to close.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all travel in Nepal has stopped, but it does show how quickly weather can turn local emergencies into wider disruption.

cover.title: Avalanche on Nepal peak leaves at least 10 missing
cover.standfirst: An avalanche struck Himlung Himal in Nepal after persistent rain and snowfall, leaving at least 10 people missing. The same weather has also caused landslides and flooding in other parts of the country, where at least one person has died. Rescue work and damage checks are still underway.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Show Himlung Himal in one engraved image split only by weather and motion, not by panels: the same identifiable ridge and corniced slope runs across the page, with the left side still intact under wind-combed snow and the right side the next instant later, the slab torn free and plunging down in white shards and debris cloud. Keep a tiny line of climbers traversing the intact section on the left; on the right, in the corresponding place, they are gone, replaced only by the moving powder blast. Hold the lower third as a mostly open snowfield with faint storm texture so type can sit cleanly.
art.note: Quiet, severe mood; cold whites, slate grey, and muted blue.
art.second_beat: First you read the mountain breaking; a beat later you realize the tiny climbers visible a moment earlier have vanished into the avalanche.

stories.headline: Measles outbreak grows in South Australia after school case
stories.dek: Health officials are tracing contacts after a teenager from Brighton Secondary School was found to have measles.
paragraphs: A measles outbreak is spreading across South Australia after a teenager from Brighton Secondary School was diagnosed with the virus. The case has pushed health officials to warn the public now because measles spreads easily through the air and can infect people before symptoms are obvious.

Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that can cause fever, rash and serious complications, especially in babies, pregnant people and those with weak immune systems. Outbreaks usually lead to contact tracing, public alerts and checks on vaccination records at schools and other places the infected person visited.

Officials have not yet said how many total cases are linked to this outbreak, where the teenager caught the virus, or how far exposure may have spread. It is also not clear whether more school communities will be affected or whether extra vaccination clinics and public health measures will follow.
stories.changes: If you were at the school or nearby exposure sites, check public health advice and make sure your measles vaccination is up to date.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean a statewide emergency, and people who are fully vaccinated are still strongly protected against serious illness.

cover.title: Measles outbreak spreads in South Australia after school case
cover.standfirst: South Australian health officials are tracing contacts after a teenager from Brighton Secondary School was diagnosed with measles. The virus spreads easily through the air, so authorities are warning people to check exposure notices, watch for symptoms and confirm their vaccinations while they look for more linked cases.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a flat, clinical background, stage two identical Australian school lunchboxes wide apart so the lower third stays empty for type. The left lunchbox is shut and ordinary; the right one has just sprung open, its lid still slightly lifted, and instead of food it contains only outbreak-response objects: a small glass thermometer, a silver blister pack, and a plain vaccination booklet/form with ruled pages and no readable text. Keep it stripped to those elements only, and make the lunchboxes unmistakably school-age and Australian in feel without logos or lettering.
art.note: Calm but alert mood, soft schoolroom colours with one sharp clinical red accent
art.second_beat: First read: two school lunchboxes; second beat: one school day has been replaced by measles-response admin and care, turning an ordinary school routine into an outbreak day.

stories.headline: US officers told to stop arrests of non-criminal immigrants
stories.dek: A reported directive also ends arrests of other undocumented people found by chance during immigration operations.
paragraphs: US immigration officers have been told to stop arresting undocumented immigrants who are not accused of crimes, according to a report published on Friday. The reported order also stops so-called collateral arrests. That means officers should not detain other undocumented people they encounter during an operation.

US immigration enforcement has often reached beyond a single target. In past operations, officers could arrest people they met at homes, workplaces or traffic stops even if those people were not the original focus. Critics said that practice spread fear in immigrant communities and discouraged people from reporting crimes or attending court.

The full wording of the directive is not public in this report, so key limits are still unclear. It is not yet known when the order takes effect, how widely it applies, or how officers will define a criminal case. Court orders, local jail cooperation and deportation proceedings may still continue.

cover.title: US officers told to stop arrests of non-criminal immigrants
cover.standfirst: A reported directive also ends arrests of other undocumented people found by chance during immigration operations.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: Show a single immigration-style dragnet being hauled sharply upward and out of frame, so only the lower arc of the mesh remains visible near the top half of the cover. In that mesh, cut one unmistakable human-shaped opening—not a generic tear, but a clean silhouette-sized gap—so it reads that the net is still being used, yet one incidental person has slipped through; keep the rest of the field empty and the lower third completely quiet for type.
art.second_beat: First you see a net in motion; then you register that the missing catch is a person-shaped escape, turning a sweep into a selective stop.

stories.headline: OpenAI halts top AI training while safety teams examine incidents
stories.dek: OpenAI said it will not restart its most advanced model training until it adds stronger safeguards and alignment checks.
paragraphs: OpenAI has paused training on its most advanced AI models, according to Axios, and says work will restart only after added safety and alignment measures are ready. The pause comes as OpenAI and Anthropic examine a large backlog of incidents found during recent testing and real-world use.

OpenAI builds large AI systems that power chatbots and other tools used by businesses and the public. Alignment work is meant to keep those systems following human instructions and limits. Axios reported that staff at OpenAI and Anthropic are reviewing tens of thousands of incidents, many of which have not been disclosed publicly.

It is still unclear how long the pause will last, which models are affected, or how serious the incidents are. Axios said early findings from company staff and outside experts have raised doubts about whether the companies can keep full control of their systems as they grow more capable.
stories.changes: For ordinary users, this could slow the arrival of more powerful AI products and put more focus on safety checks before release.
stories.unchanged: Existing AI tools are still available, and this does not mean current systems have suddenly been shut down or declared uncontrollable.

cover.title: OpenAI stops advanced AI training during broad safety review
cover.standfirst: OpenAI has paused training of its most advanced AI models and says it will resume only after adding stronger safeguards. Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic teams are reviewing tens of thousands of incidents from recent testing and real-world use, including many not yet made public.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Inside a data-centre aisle, show one towering OpenAI-style server rack missing from the middle of a tight wall of federal-blue cabinets, leaving a stark pale rectangular void like a pulled tooth. Thick unplugged cooling and power cables still swing into the empty space, while a few tiny fluorescent-pink safety reviewers on ladders and at floor level sort through a spill of incident forms and fan-fold paper exactly where the machine stood; keep the lower third mostly open with only a few sheets drifting across it. Strip out any extra room detail so the image is just the missing top-tier machine, the dangling connections, and the human safety check that has stopped everything.
art.note: Controlled alarm; limited red, black, and cool gray palette.
art.second_beat: First you see a machine has been removed; a beat later the empty slot reads as a deliberate halt in the heart of advanced training, with humans combing through the fallout before anything can be put back.

stories.headline: Madrid protest swells after 87-year-old tenant is evicted
stories.dek: Tens of thousands marched in Madrid after an elderly woman lost the apartment she had lived in for decades.
paragraphs: Tens of thousands of people marched through Madrid to protest Spain's housing crisis after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her apartment. The protest grew around one clear case. It turned a long-running housing problem into a public flashpoint this week.

Spain has faced years of tension over rents, evictions and the supply of affordable homes, especially in big cities. For many people, housing costs have risen faster than incomes. An eviction involving an elderly tenant who had lived in the same home for decades gave that pressure a human face.

It is not yet clear whether the protest will force any immediate policy change in Madrid or nationally. The unresolved issue is how Spain will protect vulnerable tenants while increasing housing supply. For renters, the risk of higher costs and displacement remains in place.
stories.changes: For ordinary renters, this protest puts more pressure on officials and landlords to answer public anger over evictions and rising housing costs.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Spain's housing rules or rents have changed yet, and one large march does not by itself stop future evictions.

cover.title: Madrid protesters rally after 87-year-old woman is evicted
cover.standfirst: Tens of thousands marched in Madrid after an 87-year-old woman was forced from the apartment where she had lived for decades. The protest focused national anger over Spain's housing crisis. What happens next depends on whether city and national leaders change eviction and rental policy.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: On a warm plain tabletop, stage the lip of a Madrid apartment doorway as a simple handmade threshold near the top half of frame, with the lower third left almost empty for type. Catch four domestic objects mid-spill off the edge into the street: a terracotta pot with a red geranium tipping first, then a small saucepan, a folded blanket, and a blue-and-white ceramic picture tile slipping after it; keep everything handmade in clay, card and felt, with the motion frozen at the instant the home starts to slide out.
art.note: Firm, public mood; red, black and dusty cream palette.
art.second_beat: First you see belongings being pushed out; second you recognise the geranium and tile as unmistakably Spanish apartment life, turning housing protest into one elderly tenant’s home being lost.
